frontmatter.title: Predicting Questionnaire Scores from Pupil, Gaze and Cursor Data

children.value: Working document (not in the table of contents), linked from
. Question: can a participant’s score on the general factor (

) or on each of the five scales be predicted out of sample from participant-level summaries of the pupil, gaze and cursor data, compared with placement behaviour and model parameters? Run 23_11, 95 participants with scores (None 37, Partial 36, Full 22).
Pupil features predict the general factor out of sample

: ridge r = .25 (95 % range over 10 CV repeats .17–.35), R² = .05 (−.02 to .12), permutation p = .006 (1,000 permutations within condition). The result holds across models: elastic net r = .26, R² = .06 (p = .010); random forest r = .27, R² = .07 (p = .010); PLS r = .28, R² = .02 (p = .006).
The same pupil block predicts STICSA trait
(r = .19, R² = .03, p = .004) and STICSA state (r = .15, R² = .00, p = .024); for the general factor they are at the permutation threshold (r = .07, p = .052).
Cursor, gaze–cursor, placement and model-parameter blocks do not predict any score
(all p ≥ .08; R² ≤ 0). Combining all blocks does not improve on the pupil block: general factor r = .07, R² = −.02 (p = .048); STICSA trait r = .19, R² = .02 (p = .008).
The pupil prediction rests mainly on a few features

, stable across folds: the feedback-pupil response to surprise, the pupil before the outcome (ISI), the feedback pupil on the trial after an event and the coupling of the attack pupil with the subsequent placement shift. The 9 model-based pupil couplings alone give r = .28, R² = .07 (p = .001); the 17 model-free pupil summaries alone r = .14, R² = .00 (p = .022).
The variance explained is small (R² ≤ .07): the scores can be predicted above chance from the pupil, but not precisely enough to estimate an individual’s score.

Self-report measures (affect ratings, post-task questions) are not used as features. The condition is entered as two dummies in every model.

), fitted inside each outer training fold: columns without training data dropped, median imputation of missing values (participants without pupil or gaze data are imputed, not dropped), standardisation, condition dummies, model. Models:
ridge (penalty chosen by efficient leave-one-out inside the training fold);
elastic net (penalty and l1 ratio by inner 3-fold CV);
random forest (300 trees, minimum leaf size 5, a third of the features per split; not tuned).
Baseline: linear regression on the condition dummies alone.

Outer CV: 5 folds stratified by condition, repeated 10 times. For each repeat, out-of-sample r is the correlation of the pooled out-of-fold predictions with the observed score, and R² = 1 − SSE / SS around the observed mean. Reported: the mean over repeats and the 2.5–97.5 % range.

The whole pipeline is rerun after permuting the score within condition: 1,000 permutations for the general factor with ridge, 500 for the scales, PLS and the interaction model. Elastic net and random forest got 100 permutations with 2 CV repeats each; a mean over fewer repeats has a wider null, so these tests are conservative. p = (1 + number of null values ≥ observed) / (1 + permutations), on the mean r.

With no signal, cross-validated r is biased below zero. The training-fold mean shifts in the opposite direction to the left-out participants, so predictions and observations are anti-correlated. Here the null means lie between −.15 and −.23, and the condition-only baseline gives r = −.07 to −.34. The relevant comparison for r is therefore the permutation null, not zero; R² > 0 is the stricter criterion.

). In each outer test fold, a feature (or a whole block) is permuted among the test participants (5 times). The drop of the pooled out-of-fold r is averaged over the 10 repeats. Stability: share of the 50 outer fits in which a feature is among the 10 largest absolute standardised ridge coefficients.

R² > 0 (mean over repeats): pupil for the general factor (.052), STICSA trait (.064), STICSA state (.037) and BDI-II (.018); gaze for STICSA trait (.032); pupil + gaze + cursor for STICSA trait (.039); all blocks for STICSA trait (.019). Every other cell has R² ≤ .001.
The PLS null is centred higher (mean about −.04 instead of −.15), so its r values are not directly comparable to the ridge values; its R² is lower than ridge’s.

In the pupil + gaze + cursor block, permuting the whole pupil block lowers r by .050 and the whole gaze block by .088; cursor (−.023) and gaze–cursor (.001) contribute nothing (

). With all blocks, pupil .037, gaze .082, model −.005, cursor −.019. The single features with the largest drop are the same pupil features (.010–.012; top-10 share .84–.96). They are followed by event-related gaze differences (other-cue gaze after events, slot entropy on event trials; .005–.009) and the event-related rate at which gaze leads the cursor (.007–.009). The gaze contribution is spread over many weakly weighted features (top-10 shares mostly < .40).

The pupil features that carry the prediction include measures whose associations with the scores were reported in the synthesis chapter for these same participants (feedback pupil × surprise, ISI pupil, attack pupil → shift). The prediction does not add a new finding about which measures relate to the scores. What it adds is that these measures, together, predict the scores out of sample better than chance, and the rest of the process data does not add to it. The feature set itself was not chosen by association with the scores: it is the complete set of pupil summaries and couplings of the pupil analysis. Whether the model-based couplings are specific to Nexus is tested in
Pupil and the Latent Signals of Three Models
: the surprise signals of the change-point observer and the n-state model give couplings with the same association with the scores.

The pattern by scale follows the loadings of the general factor: STICSA trait, STICSA state and BDI-II are predicted, IUS-12 and OCI-12 are not. The gaze block predicts STICSA trait more than the general factor.
Participants without pupil or gaze data (7–9) are predicted from imputed medians plus condition. The share of usable pupil trials is itself among the weighted features.
With R² ≤ .07, an individual’s predicted score has an error almost as large as the spread of the scores.
The participant-level feature table and predictions are kept in a local cache outside the repository.
